title: Architectural Lessons From Environmental Psychology: The Case of Biophilic Architecture
review_question: How can empirical findings from environmental psychology and aesthetics inform the design of biophilic architecture to positively influence human emotional and cognitive functioning?
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: The review synthesizes empirical findings from environmental psychology and aesthetics related to human emotional and cognitive responses to natural elements and landscape features.

findings.antecedent: Natural contents and particular landscape configurations
findings.consequent: Aesthetic attraction, positive effects on human functioning, reduced stress
findings.source: Abstract
findings.quote: humans are aesthetically attracted to natural contents and to particular landscape configurations. These features are also found to have positive effects on human functioning and can reduce stress.

findings.antecedent: Reduced opportunities for contact with natural elements in modern urban life
findings.consequent: Adverse effects on psychological and physiological well-being
findings.source: Abstract
findings.quote: this evolution can have subtle but nontrivial adverse effects on psychological and physiological well-being.

findings.antecedent: Integration of key features of natural contents and structural landscape features in the built environment (biophilic architecture)
findings.consequent: Counteraction of adverse effects on psychological and physiological well-being
findings.source: Abstract
findings.quote: These can be countered by integrating key features of natural contents and structural landscape features in the built environment.

findings.antecedent: Natural objects, shapes, and processes (e.g., ornament, structural forces)
findings.source: Introduction
findings.quote: Natural objects, shapes, and processes have often acted as a source of inspiration throughout the history of architecture.

findings.antecedent: Nature-based forms and organizations in architecture
findings.source: Introduction
findings.quote: nature-based forms and organizations in architecture are valuable for human emotional and cognitive functioning.

findings.antecedent: Environments (e.g., urban vs. natural)
findings.source: The Psychoevolutionary Framework
findings.quote: empirical evidence shows that environments (e.g., urban vs. natural) are processed according to their affective valence. Moreover, this process seems to occur very rapidly

findings.antecedent: Settings offering good opportunities for survival and reproduction
findings.source: The Psychoevolutionary Framework
findings.quote: if a setting offered good opportunities for survival and reproduction, this would have caused liking reactions, leading to explorative behavior.

findings.antecedent: Settings containing important risk (e.g., turbulent water, predator)
findings.consequent: Negatively toned affective reactions (dislike), avoidance behavior
findings.source: The Psychoevolutionary Framework
findings.quote: if early humans came across a setting containing an important risk (e.g., turbulent water, a predator), this triggered negatively toned affective reactions (e.g., dislike), ultimately leading to avoidance behavior.

findings.antecedent: Environmental features (prospect, refuge, complexity, gross structural properties, depth, ground surface/texture, absence of threats, deflected vista, coherence, legibility, mystery)
findings.consequent: Positive aesthetic evaluations, positive influence on landscape selections
findings.source: Aesthetic Preference and Structural Landscape Features
findings.quote: human beings' preference for landscapes correlates with two environmental qualities: prospect and refuge... Ulrich's psychoevolutionary framework lists some other visual cues that are associated with immediate positive affective reactions: complexity, gross structural properties (e.g., patterns), depth properties, ground surface and texture, absence of threats, and deflected vista

findings.antecedent: Natural contents (calm water features, vegetative elements like flowers and trees)
findings.source: The Aesthetic Appeal of Natural Contents
findings.quote: These benefits can explain why vegetative elements and settings containing vegetation still cause aesthetic or liking reactions. Different empirical studies show that individuals consistently prefer natural, vegetated landscapes over urban settings without vegetation.

findings.antecedent: Urban environments containing some vegetation (especially trees) or a water feature
findings.consequent: Highest preference compared to urban environments without vegetation
findings.source: The Aesthetic Appeal of Natural Contents
findings.quote: When urban environments are mutually compared, highest preference is associated with urban settings containing some vegetation, especially trees, or a water feature

findings.antecedent: Nonnatural environments (e.g., home and working interiors) containing actual vegetative elements or decorative references to natural content
findings.source: The Aesthetic Appeal of Natural Contents
findings.quote: Such phytophilia is also clear from the observation that nonnatural environments (e.g., home and working interiors) often contain actual vegetative elements or (decorative) references to natural content

findings.antecedent: Savanna-type landscapes (low to intermediately complex, grassy ground, scattered trees, high biomass, accessible, open for predator detection)
findings.source: The Savanna Hypothesis
findings.quote: The aesthetic preference for savanna-type landscapes has been the subject of a few empirical studies. Balling and Falk (1982) found that young individuals preferred savannas over other biomes without ever being exposed to the former type of landscape.

findings.antecedent: Tree shapes characteristic of high-quality savannas (low trunk, broad canopy, moderate layering)
findings.source: The Savanna Hypothesis
findings.quote: research indicates that people tend to prefer tree shapes characteristic of high-quality savannas: These typically have a low trunk, a broad canopy, and a moderate canopy layering

findings.antecedent: Natural settings
findings.consequent: Restoration of directed attention (recovery of ability to focus)
findings.source: Naturalness and Stress Reduction
findings.quote: Natural settings have been found to be ideally suited to restore or rest directed attention

findings.antecedent: Natural unthreatening (savanna-like) settings (open, low-risk, calm water, small fire, resources)
findings.consequent: Restorative responses (shift to positive emotional state, mitigation of physiological mobilization, reduced blood pressure, lower stress hormones, energy recharge)
findings.source: Naturalness and Stress Reduction
findings.quote: These restorative responses typically occurred in natural unthreatening (savanna-like) settings. Such open, low-risk environments often contained a (calm) water feature and sometimes had a small fire. Restoration was also facilitated by the availability of resources, which reduced stress related to the uncertainty of finding food

findings.antecedent: Hospital room view of a small tree group (vs. brown brick wall)
findings.consequent: Shorter hospital stays, fewer negative comments from nurses, less moderate/strong analgesics, fewer postoperative complications
findings.source: Naturalness and Stress Reduction
findings.quote: patients with the tree view had shorter hospital stays, received fewer negative comments from the nurses, required less moderate and strong analgesics, and had slightly fewer postoperative complications.

findings.antecedent: Humans' (partly) hardwired emotional affiliation with certain classes of natural objects
findings.source: The Value of Nature-Based, or Biophilic, Architecture
findings.quote: humans have a (partly) hardwired emotional affiliation with certain classes of natural objects.

findings.antecedent: Reduced contact with nature in Western technologically oriented societies
findings.consequent: Devolution of folkbiological terms, loss of precision in application, impoverishing conceptual framework for natural objects
findings.source: The Value of Nature-Based, or Biophilic, Architecture
findings.quote: Wolff, Medin, and Pankratz (1999) found that such an evolution has nontrivial effects on cultural expressions of nature. In particular, they made a historical study of word use in dictionaries and found that, from the 20th century onward, the use of (folk)biological terms devolved, and their application lost precision.

findings.antecedent: Increased presence of nonnatural artifacts (e.g., cell phones, computers, chairs, pots, printers) in human living environment
findings.consequent: Increased dominance of neural areas related to object functionality and functional analyses in thinking about the modern living environment
findings.source: The Value of Nature-Based, or Biophilic, Architecture
findings.quote: The presence of nonnatural things, and especially artifacts...is ever increasing in the human living environment at the expense of natural structures or entities. A probable consequence is that neural areas related to an object's functionality and hence functional analyses...are becoming increasingly more dominant in our thinking about the constituents of the modern living environment.

findings.antecedent: Integrating naturalistic elements in architecture (biophilic design)
findings.consequent: Counteraction of increasing dominance of functional semantic networks and associated epistemological attitude, increased attentiveness to perceptual qualities, awakening fascination for natural forms
findings.source: The Value of Nature-Based, or Biophilic, Architecture
findings.quote: integrating naturalistic elements in architecture can counteract the increasing dominance of functional semantic networks and the associated epistemological attitude...Biophilic design could lead to more attentiveness to an object's perceptual qualities, thereby leading attention away from its possible functions and the associated functionalist postures. Furthermore, because of the (hardwired) emotional affiliation with certain natural elements, nature-based architecture can awaken fascination for natural forms.

findings.antecedent: Modern urban settings (Euclidean geometry, stripped of ornament, simple volumetric forms, lack of coherence/structure)
findings.consequent: Negative feelings, stress-related endocrinal reactions, psychological and physiological costs
findings.source: The Value of Nature-Based, or Biophilic, Architecture
findings.quote: much of the modern built environment fundamentally lacks (references to) the contents and structural organization that are characteristic of a good habitat. Exposure to such environments could rapidly and automatically trigger negatively toned feelings and the associated stress-related endocrinal reactions

findings.antecedent: Architectural interventions mimicking savanna-like settings (wide/open spaces, variations in topography, clusters of real/symbolic trees, water features, small fire)
findings.consequent: Positive affect, relaxed physiological and psychological states
findings.source: Integrating Structural Landscape Features in Architecture
findings.quote: An evident strategy to imitate savannas is to integrate photographs or projections of savannas in (interior) spaces. Another, more architectural method consists of mimicking key structural features of savannas. Possible strategies include creating wide and open spaces; making variations in the architectural topography; integrating clusters of real or symbolic trees (e.g., columns); and integrating a water feature (e.g., a fountain) or even a small fire.

findings.antecedent: Architectural elements evoking prospect (larger space dimensions, raised ceilings, thin transparent walls, wide views, elevated site, increased lighting, balconies)
findings.source: Integrating Structural Landscape Features in Architecture
findings.quote: The prospect dimension depends on opposite characteristics: larger space dimensions, raised ceilings, thin transparent walls, wide views on surrounding spaces, building on an elevated site, increased lighting conditions, balconies, and so on.

findings.antecedent: Architectural elements evoking refuge/concealment (reducing lighting, lowering ceilings, small windowless spaces, thick walls)
findings.source: Integrating Structural Landscape Features in Architecture
findings.quote: Strategies for evoking concealment are reducing lighting conditions, lowering ceilings, and making small windowless spaces enclosed by thick walls.

findings.antecedent: Balanced presence of complexity and coherence in built settings
findings.source: Integrating Structural Landscape Features in Architecture
findings.quote: empirical evidence that a balanced presence of both properties contributes to the aesthetic qualities of built settings

findings.antecedent: Architectural patterns (reflectional, rotational, translational, glide symmetries, repeated/nested symmetries)
findings.source: Integrating Structural Landscape Features in Architecture
findings.quote: A possible solution is to organize these (similar) elements through patterns. These are often the result of only a few simple mathematical operations, such as reflectional, rotational, translational, and glide symmetries. More complex patterns are obtained when these symmetries are repeated or when they are nested

findings.antecedent: Architectural elements creating deflected vista (e.g., bending corridors) or enticement (partially visible objects from dark)
findings.source: Integrating Structural Landscape Features in Architecture
findings.quote: the most straightforward way to apply mystery to an architectural setting is by deflected vista. This can be realized by letting the architectural trail (e.g., corridor) bend away, which can lead to curiosity of what might lie beyond the bend, thereby encouraging explorative behavior.

findings.antecedent: Fractal patterns (vs. nonfractals)
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: Taylor mentions that more than 90% of a group of 120 students preferred fractal patterns over nonfractals.

findings.antecedent: Fractal patterns with intermediate fractal dimension (ranging from 1.3 to 1.5, or 1.4 to 1.6)
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: there is a tendency to prefer patterns with an intermediate fractal dimension, ranging from about 1.3 to 1.5.

findings.antecedent: Fractal patterns with dimension ranging from 1.2 to 1.4
findings.consequent: Best for recognizing and finding new shapes
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: Rogowitz and Voss (1990) found that recognizing and finding new shapes in fractal patterns is best for those patterns with a fractal dimension ranging from 1.2 to 1.4.

findings.antecedent: Pictures with fractal characteristics (e.g., savanna painting) with dimension 1.3 to 1.5
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: the pattern that was most effective in stress reduction, the savanna picture, had a fractal dimension that fell within the range of dimension values that was earlier found to correlate with highest aesthetic preference (Spehar et al., 2003).

findings.antecedent: Fractal dimension of landscape silhouette outlines
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: analyses showed a modest but significant correlation between mean preference and the fractal dimension of the silhouettes.

findings.antecedent: Architectural work implementing essential fractal characteristics (repeating similar details on multiple hierarchical scales, intermediate fractal dimension)
findings.consequent: Aesthetic effects, maximized for intermediate complexity, counteraction of psychological/physiological costs of Euclidean environments
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: Our preference for a specific fractal dimension further indicates that the aesthetic effects of such buildings can be maximized for intermediate levels of complexity. Perhaps this reflects our preference for intermediately complex environments, such as savannas.

findings.antecedent: Gothic architecture (porous 'holeyness', carved-out appearance, wrinkled crenelated surfaces, overall self-similarity, repetition of different shapes on different scales)
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: Goldberger (1996, p. 101) notes that "fractals capture several key features of Gothic architecture: its porous 'holeyness' or carved-out appearance, its wrinkled crenelated surfaces, and its overall self-similarity...The repetition of different shapes (arches, windows, spires) on different scales yields a combination of complexity and order.”

findings.antecedent: Hindu temples (architectural elements repeated on several scales, holographic cosmology, macrocosm encapsulated in microcosm)
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: the shape of certain Hindu temples also has conspicuous fractal characteristics...Hindu cosmology is in a sense holographic in that all parts of the cosmological whole are the whole itself and contain all the information about the whole.

findings.antecedent: Many buildings (Gothic, Baroque, Organic architecture) displaying architectural detail on different scales of magnitude
findings.source: Applying Nature's Fractal Geometry to Architecture
findings.quote: historically, architecture has always had an important fractal component (Salingaros, 2006), in that many buildings display architectural detail on different scales of magnitude, without having a more exact sense of self-similarity.

synthesis_conclusions: Humans possess a partly hardwired emotional affiliation with specific natural elements and settings, rooted in evolutionary history, which elicits positive affective and restorative responses.

Modern urban environments increasingly lack actual nature or architectural references to natural forms and structural organizations, leading to potential psychological and physiological costs, including stress and reduced well-being.

Biophilic architecture, by integrating literal imitations of natural elements, mimicking structural landscape features (e.g., savanna-like settings, prospect-refuge, complexity-coherence, mystery), and applying fractal geometry (especially with intermediate fractal dimensions), can counteract these negative effects.

These nature-based architectural interventions can promote aesthetic attraction, positive affect, stress reduction, cognitive restoration, enrich architectural design, and foster proenvironmental behavior.

The integration of fractal characteristics in architecture, particularly those with intermediate fractal dimensions (1.3-1.5), is associated with aesthetic preference and physiological stress reduction, suggesting a deeper geometric link to biophilic responses beyond literal natural content.
evidence_gaps: Further research is needed on the topic of fractal aesthetics and its possible relations to biophilia.
The exact way fractal forms contribute to restorative effects needs more investigation.
The connection between the neural basis of fractal preference (1/f noise) and the evolutionary account of biophilia needs to be clarified.
More systematic research is needed to integrate abstract structural landscape features with specific natural contents within a coherent framework.
The generalizability of aesthetic preferences (public vs. artists) needs to be considered.
limitations: Not all natural features or occurrences cause positive reactions; some can be negative or aversive.
Experimental outcomes are sometimes difficult to integrate into a coherent, overarching conceptual framework.
Differences in nature appreciation are often left in the dark in discussions.
The genetic component of positive affiliations with nature is still a matter of debate.
Biophilic architecture is not actual nature, but shares essential formal features with living things.
The argument is speculative and interdisciplinary, requiring a transdisciplinary approach.
The question of who holds the tastes (general public vs. artists) is important, as there can be discrepancies.
Innate mechanisms are open and interact with cultural/experiential parameters, meaning tastes are not exclusively dictated by biology.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Humans possess an innate tendency to connect with nature and other living systems, which is beneficial for their well-being.
Exposure to natural environments can restore directed attention, reduce mental fatigue, and improve cognitive functioning.
Exposure to natural environments can elicit physiological and psychological relaxation, leading to a reduction in stress.

mechanism_chain.description: Biophilic architectural elements, through their natural contents and configurations, engage human perceptual and cognitive systems, leading to positive affective states and restorative outcomes.

steps.from_construct: Natural contents and particular landscape configurations (biophilic architectural elements)
steps.to_construct: Perception of natural patterns, fractal dimensions, and sensory qualities (e.g., visual access to nature, natural light, natural materials)

steps.from_construct: Perception of natural patterns and sensory qualities
steps.to_construct: Positive affective responses (e.g., aesthetic attraction, feelings of pleasure, fascination) and reduced cognitive effort

steps.from_construct: Positive affective responses and reduced cognitive effort
steps.to_construct: Restoration of directed attention, reduction in physiological and psychological stress, and overall positive effects on human functioning

instruments_used.name: Perceived Restorativeness Scale (PRS)
instruments_used.description: Measures the perceived restorative qualities of an environment

instruments_used.name: Heart Rate Variability (HRV)
instruments_used.description: Measures variations in the time interval between heartbeats

instruments_used.name: Cortisol levels
instruments_used.description: Measures the concentration of the stress hormone cortisol in saliva or blood

instruments_used.name: Cognitive performance tasks
instruments_used.description: Tasks such as proofreading, digit span, or Stroop test to assess attention and executive function
